v2.name: Verb second
v2.about: In a main clause the verb comes second. Start with a time word, and the subject moves after the verb.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

v2.short: In a simple statement, the first verb comes after the first word or group of words.

perfect.name: Perfect tense: verb last
perfect.about: With hebben or zijn, the past participle goes to the end.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

perfect.short: With hebben or zijn, the form for the past, often starting with ge-, usually goes at the end of a simple sentence.

dat.name: dat: verb to the end
dat.about: After dat (that), the verb goes to the end of its clause.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Order changed in revision 2: dat needs modal, not the perfect: learners meet dat first. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

dat.short: After dat meaning “that,” put the verb at the end of that part of the sentence: Ik denk dat hij thuis is.

separable.name: Separable verbs
separable.about: Verbs like opbellen split: the verb comes second and the little word (op) goes to the end.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

separable.short: When a verb like opbellen is the only verb in a simple statement, it splits: the changing part comes second, the small word usually last.

modal.name: Modal + infinitive last
modal.about: With willen, kunnen or moeten, the second verb goes to the end.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

modal.short: With willen, kunnen, or moeten, the full verb usually goes at the end of a simple sentence.

niet.name: Where niet goes
niet.about: niet usually comes after the object, near the end.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

niet.short: Niet often comes near the end, but before a second verb or the words you are denying.

omte.name: om … te
omte.about: In order to: om, then the object, then te and the verb at the end.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

omte.short: To say what an action is for, use om, then any other words, then te and the full verb: om brood te kopen.

question.name: Questions: verb first
question.about: In a question the verb comes before the subject (after a question word, if there is one).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Order changed in revision 2: Learners need questions at once; they don't build on verb second. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

question.short: Start a yes-or-no question with the verb; after waar or wanneer, put the verb before the word for who does it.

present.name: Present tense: ik werk, jij werkt, wij werken
present.about: Most verbs use the ik form plus -t with jij/u/hij/zij/het (unless it ends in t), and the -en form with wij/jullie/zij; when jij follows the verb, use the ik form: ik werk (I work), werk jij? (work you?).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

present.short: Most verbs add -t with jij, u, hij, zij or het; wij, jullie and plural zij usually use the full verb.

de-het.name: de or het: two words for the
de-het.about: Learn each noun with de or het, both meaning the. Plurals use de: het huis (the house), de huizen (the houses).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3. Name made clearer as a title in revision 4 (the director, 2026-11-05).

de-het.short: De and het both mean “the”; learn each noun with its word, and use de for all plurals.

plural.name: Plurals with -en and -s
plural.about: Most nouns add -en or -s for the plural, sometimes with spelling changes before -en: huis → huizen (house → houses), boom → bomen (tree → trees).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

plural.short: Most nouns add -en or -s for the plural, sometimes with spelling changes: boom becomes bomen and huis becomes huizen.

geen.name: geen: no, not any
geen.about: Use geen for no, not a or not any, replacing een or going before a noun used without words like de, het or mijn: Ik heb geen auto (I have no car), we hebben geen tijd (we have no time).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3. Name made clearer as a title in revision 4 (the director, 2026-11-05).

geen.short: Use geen for “no,” “not a,” or “not any” before a noun that would otherwise have een or no word like de, het, or mijn.

er-is.name: er is and er zijn: there is and there are
er-is.about: Use er is (there is) with a noun that is not plural, and er zijn (there are) with a plural: Er is koffie (there is coffee), er zijn stoelen (there are chairs).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

er-is.short: Use er is with a noun that is not plural, and er zijn with a plural noun.

adjective.name: Adjectives with and without -e
adjective.about: Before a noun, an adjective usually adds -e, except with a het noun after een, geen or no word. When it describes the subject after zijn, it usually has no -e: een groot huis (a big house), het huis is groot (the house is big).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

adjective.short: Before a noun, a describing word usually adds -e; with a het noun that is not plural, it usually has no -e after een, geen, or no word.

diminutive.name: -je and -tje: small or friendly
diminutive.about: Use -je, -tje, -pje, -etje or -kje to make a noun sound small or friendly. The ending depends on the noun; use het unless the noun is plural: het huisje (the little house), het boompje (the little tree).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

diminutive.short: Add an ending such as -je or -tje to make a noun sound small or friendly; use het when it is not plural and de when it is plural.

past.name: Past tense: werkte, woonde, ging
past.about: For many verbs, add -te or -de to the ik form for the past, with another -n for wij/jullie/zij. Other verbs change more: Ik werkte hier (I worked here), wij gingen weg (we went away).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

past.short: Many verbs add -te or -de for the past, plus -n with wij, jullie, or plural zij; others change, like gaan → ging.

omdat.name: omdat, als and more: verb last
omdat.about: After words such as omdat (because), als (if/when), wanneer (when), toen (when in the past), terwijl (while), voordat (before) and of (whether), put the verb at the end of that part of the sentence: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik moe ben (I stay home because I tired am).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

omdat.short: After words such as omdat, als, wanneer, toen, terwijl, voordat, and of meaning “whether,” the verb goes to the end of that part of the sentence.

relative.name: die and dat: who, which, that
relative.about: To add who, which or that after a noun, use die with nouns that take de and dat with nouns that take het; put the verb last in that part of the sentence: de man die hier woont (the man who here lives), het boek dat ik lees (the book that I read).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

relative.short: To add “who,” “which,” or “that” after a noun, use die for de nouns and dat for het nouns, with the verb at the end.

imperative.name: Commands: kom hier
imperative.about: Commands usually use the ik form without ik: Kom hier (come here), doe de deur dicht (do the door shut).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

imperative.short: For most commands, use the form used with ik and leave out ik: kom hier, pak je tas.

reflexive.name: Verbs with me, je, zich and ons
reflexive.about: Some verbs, including those for hurrying and remembering, need me with ik, je with jij/jullie, zich with hij/zij/het/u or plural zij, and ons with wij: Ik verveel me (I bore myself), ik herinner me dat (I remember myself that).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

reflexive.short: Some verbs need an extra word that matches who does it: ik verveel me, jij verveelt je, wij vervelen ons.

comparative.name: Comparisons: -er, meer, het -st, het meest
comparative.about: Usually add -er for more; with zijn and no following noun, use het …-st for most. Some words use meer/het meest, dan means than, and a few change form: goed → beter → best (good → better → best), dit is groter dan dat (this is bigger than that).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

comparative.short: Usually add -er to compare, use het …-st after zijn for the highest degree, and use dan for “than.”

future.name: gaan and zullen: talking about the future
future.about: With another verb at the end, gaan can express a plan and zullen a promise or prediction: Ik ga morgen koken (I go tomorrow cook), ik zal je helpen (I will you help).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

future.short: Gaan can introduce a plan; zullen can introduce a promise or prediction. The full verb usually goes at the end.

object.name: me, je, hem: object words
object.about: Object words include me/mij, je/jou, hem, haar, het, ons, jullie and ze. In a sentence starting with the subject, they usually follow the first verb: Ik zie hem (I see him), ik geef ze geld (I give them money).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

object.short: Use me, je, hem, haar, het, ons, jullie, or ze for who or what an action affects; they usually follow the first verb.

possessive.name: mijn, jouw, ons: words for belonging
possessive.about: Use mijn (my), jouw/je (your), zijn (his/its), haar (her), ons/onze (our), jullie (your, plural), hun (their) and uw (your, polite). Use ons with a noun that takes het, and onze with de or plurals: ons huis (our house), onze fietsen (our bikes).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

possessive.short: Words such as mijn and jouw show who something belongs to; “our” is ons with het nouns and onze with de nouns or plurals.

aan-het.name: zijn + aan het: happening right now
aan-het.about: To say what is happening right now, use a form of zijn + aan het + the full verb: Ik ben aan het koken (I am at the cooking), ze zijn aan het eten (they are at the eating).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

aan-het.short: Use a form of zijn + aan het + the full verb to say an activity is happening right now.

time-place.name: Time, then how, then where
time-place.about: When time, how and place appear together, the usual order is time, how, place; English often puts time last: Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Utrecht (I go tomorrow with the train to Utrecht).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

time-place.short: When time, how, and place come together, the usual order is time, how, then place.

zijn-hebben.name: zijn and hebben: ik ben, ik heb
zijn-hebben.about: The two most used verbs have their own forms: ik ben, jij bent, hij is, wij zijn; ik heb, jij hebt, hij heeft, wij hebben (u bent; u hebt or u heeft): Ik ben moe (I am tired), ze heeft een auto (she has a car).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

zijn-hebben.short: Zijn and hebben have their own forms: ik ben/heb, jij bent/hebt, hij is/heeft, and wij zijn/hebben.

demonstrative.name: deze, die, dit, dat: this and that
demonstrative.about: Use deze (this/these) and die (that/those) with nouns that take de or are plural, and dit (this) and dat (that) with nouns that take het: dit huis (this house), die boeken (those books).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3.

demonstrative.short: Use deze and die with de nouns or plurals; use dit and dat with het nouns that are not plural.

want.name: want: because, with the usual order
want.about: To join sentences that have the verb second, use en (and), maar (but) or want (because). Each part keeps that order: Ik blijf thuis, want ik ben moe (I stay home, because I am tired).

source.reviewed: 3 rounds by gpt-6-astra, as a native-speaker teacher
source.note: Order changed in revision 2: want keeps the usual order, so it doesn't build on omdat. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 3. Name made clearer as a title in revision 4 (the director, 2026-11-05).

want.short: When en, maar, or want joins two statements, each part keeps its usual word order.
